### Also covered by

Fong & Spivak, *Seven Sketches in Compositionality* (CUP, 2019), §3.2.1 Exercise 3.10, printed p. 83 (PDF p. 95) — item `7sketches:3.2.1:ex3.10`. Seven Sketches introduces the same category `3` as the free category on the linear three-vertex graph and asks for its complete multiplication table, which goes one step beyond settling freeness.

- [ ] (from Seven Sketches §3.2.1) Enumerate the six morphisms of the category `3` — three identities, the two generators, and their composite — and prove the full composition table: every defined composite computed, every identity entry identified, and equality of morphisms decided.

### Also covered by

Fong & Spivak, *Seven Sketches in Compositionality* (CUP, 2019), §3.2.1 Exercise 3.12, printed p. 83 (PDF p. 95) — item `7sketches:3.2.1:ex3.12`. Parts (1) and (2) of the exercise (the categories `1` and `0`) are already in tree as `Instance/One.v:25` and `Instance/Zero.v:28`, and the agreement isomorphisms are already on this issue's checklist. Part (3) asks for something this issue does not yet name: a closed formula for the number of morphisms of the n-th member of the family.

- [ ] (from Seven Sketches §3.2.1) Prove the morphism count of `[n]`: its hom-sets are jointly in bijection with the pairs i ≤ j drawn from n elements, so `[n]` has n(n+1)/2 morphisms — a closed formula proved by induction, not an enumeration produced separately for each n.

### Also covered by

Fong & Spivak, *Seven Sketches in Compositionality* (CUP, 2019), §3.2.1 Example 3.13, printed p. 83 (PDF p. 95) — item `7sketches:3.2.1:example3.13`. Seven Sketches states the same correspondence in both directions: a category with a single object is the same thing as a monoid, taking the hom-set at that object as carrier, the identity as unit, and composition as multiplication, with the monoid laws being exactly the category laws.

No new checkbox: this is already the scope of this issue's delooping construction together with its `hom(a, a)`-is-a-monoid converse. The only thing the Seven Sketches reading adds is a presentational request — that the two be delivered as a *correspondence* (a named statement that the constructions are mutually inverse) rather than as two unrelated constructions sitting side by side.

Separately, the concrete instance Example 3.13 leads with — the free category on a one-vertex one-loop graph, whose hom-set is in bijection with the naturals under addition — is filed as its own Seven Sketches §3.2.1 issue, which depends on this one.

### Also covered by

Fong & Spivak, *Seven Sketches in Compositionality* (CUP, 2019), §3.2.2, the unnumbered definition of a path equation, a finite presentation, and a finitely presented category, printed p. 84 (PDF p. 96) — item `7sketches:3.2.2:def-finite-presentation`. This is the same obligation as this issue's presented-category construction, but Seven Sketches adds two qualifiers that the current checklist does not name.

- [ ] (from Seven Sketches §3.2.2) Restrict imposed equations to PARALLEL paths: an equation may be imposed only between paths sharing both source and target, so the relation is indexed by a source and a target and an equation between non-parallel paths is not expressible. Record the consequence the book draws — imposing equations can only merge morphisms, never add them — as a lemma about the projection (bijective on objects, surjective on each hom-set).
- [ ] (from Seven Sketches §3.2.2) Define `FinitelyPresented`: a presentation whose generating quiver has finitely many nodes and edges and whose equation set is finite, carried as *data* (enumerations) rather than as an existence claim, so no choice principle is needed.

### Also covered by

Fong & Spivak, *Seven Sketches in Compositionality* (CUP, 2019), §3.2.2 Example 3.18, printed pp. 84–85 (PDF pp. 96–97) — item `7sketches:3.2.2:example3.18`. The example presents the same one-object category by a single generator subject to the relation that its square is the identity, and uses it to make the point that imposing one equation forces further ones.

- [ ] (from Seven Sketches §3.2.2) For the presentation ⟨s | s ∘ s = id⟩, prove the *derived* equations explicitly (the cube is the generator, the fourth power is the identity) and then the collapse: the presented category has exactly the two morphisms {id, s}, with the enumeration proved and equality of words decided. Identify the result with the group already built at `Instance/Comp.v:405`, so the presentation and the equational construction are related rather than left as two unconnected objects.

### Also covered by

Fong & Spivak, *Seven Sketches in Compositionality* (CUP, 2019), §3.2.2 Exercise 3.19, printed p. 85 (PDF p. 97) — item `7sketches:3.2.2:ex3.19`. This asks for a one-object presented category outside the family this issue currently lists: the generator is subject to a relation between two *powers*, neither of which is the identity, so the result is a monoid with a tail rather than a cyclic group.

- [ ] (from Seven Sketches §3.2.2, Exercise 3.19) Add the one-object presentation ⟨s | s⁵ = s²⟩ and prove its morphism set is exactly {id, s, s², s³, s⁴}, with the fifth power equal to the second — i.e. a five-element monoid with a two-step tail and a three-element cycle. The enumeration and a decision procedure for equality of words are the content; note in passing that this monoid is not a group, unlike every other example in this issue.

### Also covered by

Fong & Spivak, *Seven Sketches in Compositionality* (CUP, 2019), §3.3.5, the extended example presenting the category of graphs as a functor category, printed pp. 97–99 (PDF pp. 109–111) — item `7sketches:3.3.5:construction-gr`. This is the same identification as this issue's: instances on the two-vertex, two-parallel-arrow schema are graphs, and their natural transformations are graph homomorphisms, the two naturality squares saying exactly that endpoints are preserved.

One orientation note and one correction, both worth carrying into the issue body. Seven Sketches uses the COVARIANT reading (the schema has arrows from the arrow-object to the vertex-object, and an instance is a covariant functor to sets), whereas this issue states the identification against `[Parallel^op, Sets]`; the two agree, but the agreement should be recorded rather than assumed. And the in-tree state is better than a first reading suggests: `Instance/Parallel.v:129` `APair` already constructs an instance from any parallel pair, in the book's own variance, so "graph data yields an instance" exists generically — `Presheaf_Graph` (`Instance/Parallel.v:166`) being defined once and referenced nowhere is not evidence to the contrary.

- [ ] (from Seven Sketches §3.3.5) Record the identification in the covariant orientation as well (or prove the two orientations agree), since the schema as the book presents it is covariant and downstream Chapter 3 material — the schema functors of §3.4.1 — is written in that variance.
